title: 38 countries climbed into high income. Only one from East & Southeast Asia

voiceover.text: Since nineteen eighty-eight, thirty-eight countries have climbed into high income.
From East and Southeast Asia? Just one.
The World Bank draws the high-income line at about fourteen thousand dollars a person. And countries didn't cross it one by one. They came in waves.
First, Central and Eastern Europe. Eight countries, as the EU grew east.
Then the commodity boom. Chile, Brazil, Argentina, Russia, Venezuela.
But many didn't stay. Within five years, Brazil, Venezuela, Russia and Kazakhstan had all fallen back.
Argentina has crossed the line three times. Today, it's just thirty-five dollars above it.
The fastest climb of all? Guyana. Oil started flowing, and income per person went from six thousand four hundred dollars to almost thirty thousand, in five years.
Still, thirty-three of the thirty-eight are above the line today. So what does a climb that sticks look like?
South Korea crossed in ninety-two. The Asian crisis knocked it back. A year later it returned, and never left.
In twenty eleven, Thailand and China were neck and neck. Both under half the line.
Today, China is at ninety-five percent.
Thailand reached fifty-three percent in twenty seventeen. Seven years later, it's right back there.
We found this on Querious, by comparing open World Bank data with each year's income line.
Find every crossing, then download the result, or connect it to your own tools.
The data is open. The question is yours.
